title: A Benedictine day at home
hookLine: a bell, a psalm, work, reading, a meal, silence

cards: Six things. A bell. A psalm.
Silence. That's the whole list, and it's almost too plain to write down. But lay those six out across a day and something happens to the day.
It stops being one long smear of tasks and screens and becomes a set of rooms, each with a door.

teach.h: THE BELL: THE NEXT THING HAS COME.
teach.b: Start with the bell. In the Rule, the bell isn't a nag.
It's a signal that the next thing has come, and at the signal for prayer, Benedict says, monks put down whatever is in their hands and go: nothing before the work of God.
At home the bell might be an alarm, the kettle, a church bell down the street. Then the psalm.
The monks pray at set hours, from the night office to the last prayer before sleep; at home it may be one psalm, morning or evening. Then work.
Idleness, Benedict writes, is the enemy of the soul, so there are hours for work with the hands, and the tools are handled like the vessels of the altar.
Then reading: hours set aside for slow, attentive reading of Scripture. Then a meal, eaten with others while someone reads aloud, with food and drink that's enough and not too much.
Then silence, especially after the last prayer at night. The thread through every piece is balance. Benedict keeps asking for measure.

teach.h: SOMETHING FOR THE STRONG, NOTHING TO FLEE.
teach.b: He wants the abbot to arrange everything so that the strong have something to strive for and the weak have nothing to run from. Prayer doesn't swallow work. Work doesn't swallow reading.
In chapter sixty-four, Benedict calls this good judgment discretion, the mother of virtues.
So the Benedictine day isn't impressive. It's proportioned. Tomorrow the path leaves the monastery and walks out on the road with Francis of Assisi.

how: Some Benedictine oblates and other laypeople shape their day around short times of the Liturgy of the Hours, a period of lectio divina, focused work and shared meals, adapted to family and job.

games.q: what does “a benedictine day at home” mean?
o: a day shaped by prayer, work, reading and rest, in balance
a day of strict silence and fasting from dawn to dark
a retreat day spent as a guest inside a real monastery

games.q: the Benedictine day — tap the pairs.

s: Benedict's Rule asks for heroic extremes of fasting and prayer
the abbot is to arrange things so the strong have something to strive for and the weak nothing to run from.
at the signal for prayer, monks put down what they're doing
nothing is to be put before the work of God.
in the Rule, reading is something done only on feast days
hours are set aside for reading in the ordinary rhythm of the day.

games.q: you're the abbot. some brothers are strong and eager, some are tired and frail. how do you set the demands of the day?
o: set them high, so only the strong stay.
set them low, so nobody is ever stretched.
arrange them so the strong have something to strive for and the weak nothing to run from.
games.why: chapter sixty-four asks the abbot for exactly this, and calls the good judgment behind it discretion, the mother of virtues.

practice: Look at the rest of your day and choose one hour you could shape: a psalm, then work with no phone in reach, a short stretch of reading, a meal eaten slowly.
For now, rest in the silence that ends a Benedictine day, and when this session's bell rings, take it the way the Rule does: the next thing has come.

wordCard.voice: A Benedictine day at home. Bell, psalm, work, reading, meal and silence, kept in balance, the way the Rule shapes a monk's hours, brought into an ordinary house. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: discretion, good judgment, which Benedict calls the mother of virtues in chapter sixty-four.

carryVoice: Your line: balance. Discretion keeps each piece in its place. That's the last day with Benedict.
